item.title: Six AGIBOT G2 Robots Complete 1,730 Tasks in 24-Hour Shanghai Convenience Store Trial
item.dc:creator: Sponsored Content
item.description:
Four of the six robots pass a performance assessment as the trial puts customer service, retail operations and embodied AI capabilities to the test in a working store.

The post Six AGIBOT G2 Robots Complete 1,730 Tasks in 24-Hour Shanghai Convenience Store Trial appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Four of the six robots pass a performance assessment as the trial puts customer service, retail operations and embodied AI capabilities to the test in a working store. 

Six AGIBOT G2 wheeled humanoid robots completed a 24-hour trial at an operating convenience store in Shanghai’s Xuhui District, performing a combined 1,730 tasks ranging from customer assistance and coffee preparation to shelf restocking and cleaning.

The trial ran from 10 a.m. on November 2 to 10 a.m. on November 3 and was livestreamed to an audience of more than two million viewers across online platforms. Four of the six robots passed the final performance assessment.

The event marked the conclusion of AGIBOT’s AI WAVE technology showcase, launched on October 22. Following a series of releases spanning robotics data, simulation, AI models, hardware and operational software, the convenience store trial brought these technologies together in a real-world setting to examine how robots perform everyday tasks over an extended operating period. More broadly, the trial showed how embodied AI could move beyond controlled demonstrations and operate in the changing conditions of a live, customer-facing environment.

Six Robots Take on Everyday Store Operations

The six G2 robots were assigned different responsibilities: customer assistance, shelf inspections, restocking, coffee preparation, checkout and hot food service, and store cleaning.

Over the 24-hour period, they completed 683 customer-service interactions, 369 product pickups and deliveries, 147 coffee orders, 126 breakfast servings, 277 shelf inspections and restocking tasks, and 128 table-cleaning tasks.

The trial covered four operating periods: the lunchtime rush, evening peak hours, overnight operations and the following morning’s breakfast rush. Each period brought different demands, from handling customer requests during busy hours to maintaining store operations overnight.

The robots were assessed on their time on duty, task completion, customer feedback, response times and ability to handle unexpected situations. Four passed the final assessment, while two did not meet all the criteria.

Two evaluators also conducted rounds of practical tests based on situations robots might encounter while serving customers. In one test, they ordered regular and sugar-free Coca-Cola to check whether the robots could distinguish between similar-looking products. In another, they rearranged packs of chewing gum on a shelf and asked the robots to return them to their correct positions.

The evaluators also blocked an aisle with a person and a box to test whether the robots could identify obstacles and navigate around them.

Real-World Retail Tasks Test Precision and Adaptability

A convenience store may appear to be a relatively straightforward environment for robots. Its layout is compact and many tasks follow standard procedures. Yet everyday activities such as picking up products, restocking shelves and preparing food require robots to adapt to small but frequent changes.

A bag of candy hanging at a slightly different angle can be difficult to grasp without disturbing nearby products. Handling a delicate item, such as a slice of cake, requires careful control of gripping force to avoid dropping or damaging it.

Unlike a controlled laboratory, an operating store presents constantly changing conditions. Customers move through the aisles, products are picked up and returned, and items vary in position, orientation and packaging. Even when a robot repeats the same task, the conditions may differ from one attempt to the next.

During the trial, the G2 robots demonstrated several capabilities designed to address these challenges. They used real-time visual information to identify misplaced merchandise and return it to designated shelf positions rather than relying solely on preset coordinates.

A robot assigned to restocking detected gaps on shelves and replenished products without a specific prompt. In the cleaning area, another robot distinguished spills from countertop patterns and selected appropriate tools for cleaning.

These tasks tested more than individual movements. They required the robots to perceive their surroundings, make task-specific decisions and adjust their actions as conditions changed.

Genie Master Connects Robot Actions with Continuous Improvement

The trial also tested how AGIBOT’s Genie Master embodied AI agent framework could support task coordination, error correction and learning from operational experience.

Even routine store tasks do not always go as planned. A robot may fail to grasp an item correctly, encounter an unexpected obstacle or need to adjust its movements. Beyond completing individual tasks, the trial examined how robots could respond to these situations and use the resulting feedback to improve future performance.

Genie Master provides a shared framework for coordinating the six robots and connecting their actions with subsequent analysis and learning.

Through the Embodied Execution Protocol (EEP), Genie Master links task planning, execution and feedback. The system organizes work according to each robot’s capabilities and the conditions in the store. Robots then perform their assigned tasks using action policies and real-time observations, with execution results returned to Genie Master for analysis and troubleshooting.

The framework also supports learning from previous attempts. By reviewing successful and unsuccessful task executions, it can retain relevant experience in long-term memory for use in similar situations. Effective adjustments can also be converted into training data to help refine the robots’ action policies.
This approach is intended to help robots build on previous experience rather than treating each task as an isolated operation. AGIBOT has been using operational feedback to improve G2 performance on tasks requiring precise manipulation, including additional practice during quieter overnight periods.
Plans to Expand Testing Across Real-World Applications

The convenience store trial brought together AGIBOT’s robotics hardware, AI models, simulation technologies and operational systems in a single working environment.

Beyond the number of tasks completed, the trial examined practical questions about robot performance: whether robots could carry out assigned duties over an extended period, how they responded to unexpected problems and whether experience gained from previous tasks could be applied to new situations.

AGIBOT plans to continue testing its robots across additional roles and real-world environments, using operational feedback to improve reliability, task execution and adaptability.

As robots take on a wider range of responsibilities, the company will also assess which capabilities and operating practices can be transferred between tasks and replicated across different settings. These findings will help guide the next stage of development toward more consistent and scalable real-world deployment.

item.title: How Rhoda AI is using video data to create generalized AI models for robots
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Rhoda AI offers a direct video action model, which it recently extended with mobile DVA, to enable robots to understand the physical world.

The post How Rhoda AI is using video data to create generalized AI models for robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Rhoda pretrains its models on internet-scale video to build a strong prior on motion, physics, and physical interaction. | Source: Rhoda AI

Earlier this year, Rhoda AI emerged from 18 months of stealth with $450 million in Series A funding. The company is working with customers in automotive, manufacturing, logistics, and e-commerce to deploy its direct video action, or DVA, model for robotics.

“We’re focused on deploying in the real world, and that means you have to deal with the messiness of the real world. Every run can be different,” Jagdeep Singh, the co-founder and CEO of Rhoda AI, told The Robot Report. “Every configuration can be different, and you need a really robust model. To build a robust model, you need a massive training dataset.”

A large training dataset is exactly what allowed large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT to rapidly progress in recent years. Physical AI has trailed behind those models because the same dataset doesn’t exist for the physical world, noted Singh.

“Every word ever put on the internet, from Shakespeare to Reddit, was used to train these AI models. In the physical AI world, you didn’t have an internet-scale dataset,” he said. “People tried to collect their own data by tele-operating robots, and that approach made for interesting lab demonstrations in robots that could fold T-shirts or make coffees and so on, but none of those demonstrations were robust enough to cross over into the real world. The number of autonomous manipulation capable robots that are solving real world problems today is effectively zero.”

Rhoda AI is betting on using video to data to close this gap and to create truly generalized robotics.

How does a DVA model work?

Many physical AI developers are creating vision-language-action (VLA) models, which allow robots to learn from data from images or videos of its surroundings and text instructions. These models, however, still struggle to cope with the variability of the real world, according to Rhoda AI.

The company claimed that its DVA model, which it recently extended with mobile DVA, combines manipulation and mobility into one policy.

“The way it works is the model will look at a history of video frames and action tokens and language tokens. From that history, or from that context, it will make a prediction in video for the next few 100 milliseconds, the next half second or so,” explained Singh. “It’ll predict the scene and what it thinks will happen in that scene. Once you have that prediction, you pass it to a second part of the model, which is an action converter. It takes the video scene and spits out robot actions.”

“Once you have that action space output, you can execute those actions on a real robot. The robot then moves for that half second, and then you make a new observation, because the state of the world has changed, and you make a new prediction for the next half second,” he continued. “It’s basically making an observation, a prediction of what should happen next, a conversion to action, an execution of the action, and then you close the loop and make a new observation and a new prediction based on that new observation.”

For Rhoda AI, quantity of data is key

According to Singh, any AI model that’s trained on a small dataset is going to be very brittle. These models could work if the inference time distribution of data is very similar to the training time distribution, but as those distributions diverge, then the model starts to fail.

“Hundreds of years of videos were used to train the model, so the model has seen just an incredible diversity of everything: baseball videos, people throwing darts, waves crashing on a beach, or trees blowing in the wind,” Singh said. “Not just videos that have humans in them. Every video has something to teach the model about how the world works. Essentially, the entire internet becomes like a physics classroom.”

Rhoda AI uses video data for pretraining. “Once you’ve gotten that pretraining, you then apply a small amount of task-specific training, maybe 10 to 20 hours’ worth, similar to the way you would train a new worker on an assembly line,” said Singh. “They already come in with a certain set of skills, and you need to teach them the workflow of your particular company. With that little bit of post training, the model is able to do things that traditional robots cannot do.”

The Palo Alto, Calif.-based company aims to make a model that can understand the world generally. For this, it doesn’t limit the data it uses to just human-centric videos.

“We looked at more heavily curated videos that only had human, egocentric manipulation in them,” Singh said. “There was a question of maybe those videos were better to train on. We found that the models that perform the best were the ones actually trained on the broadest data sets, including things that were not obviously relevant to manipulation.”

This generalization also enables Rhoda AI’s models to generalize across different robot embodiments. In fact, the specific robot embodiment only comes into play in the post-training phase.

How does Rhoda AI offer its models?

Singh said Rhoda AI is a full-stack company, and it offers its technology in a range of methods.

“We always own the AI layer, that’s the core,” Singh said. “In terms of the body or hardware layer, we can run with our body or a third-party body. In terms of the skills, we can be the ones training the skills, or we can let third parties train the skills. That provides the largest set of solutions to our customers, and that’s really our mission.”

Internally, Rhoda AI is focusing on developing skills in manufacturing and logistics.

“We’re going after those areas because there’s an immediate problem there,” added Singh. “Many manufacturing and logistics companies have a shortage of labor. Many industries have been offshored for decades because its too expensive to build in those economies. So this technology offers a path to repatriate some of those industries.”

Looking ahead, Rhoda AI aims to continue getting its model out into the real world. Singh said he believes robotics’ “ChatGPT moment” will be coming sooners than people expect.

“The kind of approach we’re taking really has the potential to get us there because the only way to get that level of generality is to train on a dataset that has both the scale of the internet and diversity of the internet,” said Singh. “If you don’t have both those things, your models will not be able to generalize well enough.”

item.title: Narwal builds robot vacuums to serve regional needs
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
Narwal executives say they spent a decade in research and development and have tailored their household cleaning robots to local markets.

The post Narwal builds robot vacuums to serve regional needs appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Narwal has designed robots that can both vacuum and mop. Source: Narwal

Robots have entered homes, but the path to consumer adoption has been long and winding. iRobot Corp. was the pioneer but entered bankruptcy proceedings late in 2025. Narwal Robotics Corp. has spent a decade on research and development, testing 30 technical routes to self-cleaning robotic mops, and building a supply chain to retain cost control.

While iRobot has emerged from bankruptcy with a new owner, Narwal is working toward an initial public offering (IPO). The company, which has offices in Shenzhen, China, and Covina, Calif., is looking to embodied intelligence to take home robots from the “iPod stage” to the “iPhone moment,” according to founder and CEO Junbin Zhang.

Zhang and Icey Bin, head of global brand at Narwal, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report:

Narwal took time to understand the household space

Why has the household robotics market been so difficult to break into?

The household robotics market has exceptionally high barriers to entry in R&D, supply chain, and algorithm development. In the early days, there were no mature industry solutions to reference. For instance, Narwal spent three years with zero revenue solely focused on R&D, iterating the self-cleaning mop structure over 10 times from scratch.

Additionally, contract manufacturers were initially reluctant to cooperate due to the complex product structures and low initial volumes. On the software side, features like automatic mop washing require extremely precise positioning algorithms for the robot to frequently return to its base station, which the industry lacked at the time.

Most importantly, to achieve a high market penetration, a company must refine the product’s experience, quality, and cost to the reliable standards of mature home appliances, which is an incredibly difficult ceiling to break through.

iRobot struggled for a number of reasons. Haven’t other vacuum providers such as Dyson picked up market share?

Over the past decade, the core dimension of industry competition has fundamentally shifted from stacking hardware parameters to delivering a low-intervention, automated cleaning experience. While traditional handheld vacuums still have a place, overseas households face complex pain points that require automated solutions—such as deep cleaning for carpets and managing pet hair.

To address this, Narwal innovated a dedicated carpet deep-cleaning module that automatically lifts the mop and increases suction, boosting carpet cleaning performance by 40% to 50% compared to traditional models.

Furthermore, we pioneered the DualFlow tangle-free system to fundamentally solve the pet hair tangling issue. This paradigm shift toward comprehensive automation and solving highly specific pain points is why Chinese challengers have reshaped the global market landscape.

Submit your innovation now!

Technology and supply chain were built from scratch

How is Narwal’s technology and business model different from those of existing cleaning robot players?

Narwal stands out from incumbent players by rejecting the industry playbook of parameter stacking and scale-first growth, instead building original, user value-centered innovations across four core dimensions:

  1. Technology route: category-defining innovation from scratch: Instead of incremental upgrades to basic sweeping functions, Narwal created the entire self-cleaning robot mop category from its first product. Its proprietary technology portfolio — including self-developed SLAM algorithms, NarMind autonomous system, FlowWash hot water cleaning, and DualFlow tangle-free system — all target universal industry pain points rather than meaningless parameter competition.
  2. A model with full end-to-end control of the supply chain: Unlike the prevalent asset-light, OEM-heavy model, Narwal leverages the mature Greater Bay Area, a leading comprehensive manufacturing hub in southern China. Its full “Shenzhen R&D + Dongguan manufacturing” setup covers the full product lifecycle from development and design to manufacturing and delivery, enabling faster product iteration and consistent quality control.
  3. Operating logic: refined long-term management: Narwal rejects short-term tactics such as exchanging losses for market share and eroding brand value through price wars. It operates under a business-unit structure where R&D and frontline teams function as mutual profit centers, balancing innovation investment and market demand to avoid blind feature stacking or ineffective marketing spending.
  4. Strategic path: experience-first penetration: Contrary to the “chasing scale first, fixing experience later” industry norm, Narwal follows a long-term experience-first strategy: it polishes floor cleaning performance to mature home appliance standards first, then gradually reduces costs and drives market penetration through supply chain optimization, with the goal of turning robot vacuums from tech novelties into household essentials.

In what geographic regions have you found the most traction and why?

To date, Narwal’s products have entered more than 30 countries and regions globally, reaching over 6 million users. We have seen significant traction across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East.

Between January and April 2026, our overseas revenue grew by nearly 50% year-on-year. This success is primarily because we practice a “one country, one policy” approach, heavily customizing product features based on local lifestyle needs.

In North America, the U.S. is one of our most important markets. Our Flow 2 claimed the No. 1 spot in the robot vacuum new release category on Amazon U.S. within 24 hours of launch, with sales up 305% year over year versus the previous generation.

Key local optimizations include battery capacity and path planning upgrades for large single-family homes, plus a dedicated carpet deep-clean mode and DualFlow tangle-free system roller brush tailored to the high pet ownership rate. We have also established offline retail partnerships with major national chains including Best Buy and Costco.

In Europe, we have expanded steadily since 2024. During the 2025 Black Friday period, revenue in the French market surged 449% year on year, and first-launch sales across Europe grew 241% year on year.

Key local optimizations are enhanced carpet-cleaning performance and DualFlow tangle-free system for pet households, as well as water system adjustments for hard-water regions. We have a direct presence via our official website and Amazon in France, Italy, and Germany, with extended reach in Spain, Sweden, and the Netherlands, plus an extensive offline retail network.

Narwal address AI and privacy concerns

How do you see recent AI advances enabling more applications for consumer robots?

Recent AI advances are transforming consumer robots from executing “command-based cleaning” to performing “perception-based intelligent cleaning.” For example, Narwal pioneered the AI DirtSense technology and FlowWash hot water cleaning to sense floor dirt levels and automatically adjust cleaning power.

Furthermore, we were the first to mass-produce robot vacuums with dual-camera vision, allowing robots to achieve precise environment perception, obstacle avoidance, and scene recognition. Additionally, large language models enable natural language dialogue, allowing users to issue complex commands like “clean up the melon seeds near the sofa” instead of rigid keywords

When you mention “3D embodied intelligence,” how do you avoid the privacy concerns that affected iRobot?

Data privacy and security are core commitments across every market we operate in, and we have built multi-layer safeguards to address privacy risks. Beyond data governance, most of our products have obtained TÜV certification for product safety and quality as part of our broader commitment to being a trusted brand in people’s homes.

Minimized data collection by design: Our privacy policy explicitly states that Narwal does not automatically collect user photos or videos without user consent and affirmative user action. Sensitive network information, such as Wi-Fi passwords, is stored locally on the user’s robot and app only, and is never uploaded to our cloud servers.

Personal information collected is only used for necessary purposes, including providing product services, verifying accounts, optimizing product experience, ensuring security, and complying with legal obligations. We never repurpose it for unrelated uses.

Full regulatory compliance: Our products and services comply with applicable data protection laws and regulations in all operating markets, including GDPR in the EU/EEA and CPRA in California.

Cleaning robots are tailored for the U.S. market

How are you navigating tariffs and the recent  FCC restrictions? How do you ensure a reliable supply chain?

Regarding the FCC’s action, we want to assure our customers that Narwal’s current lineup is not impacted—every model sold in the U.S. today remains fully certified, fully supported, and available at retail. For future products, we are closely reviewing the FCC’s announcement, including the conditional approval process.

As for tariffs, we are currently evaluating what these new requirements would mean for our operations. To ensure a highly reliable supply chain, Narwal relies on an “end-to-end” closed-loop talent and manufacturing system based in the China Greater Bay Area. While overseas competitors might take months to prototype a product, our highly clustered supply chain lets us prototype and iterate within a week, giving us the efficiency to weather external shocks.

Are you customizing any features for the U.S. market?

Yes, we have customized products and operations for the U.S. market across product performance, scenario adaptation and compliance dimensions:

Cleaning scenario adaptation: For the high pet ownership rate in the U.S. market, we optimized the DualFlow tangle-free system roller brush to effectively solve the pet hair tangling pain point.

For the high carpet coverage rate, we launched a Carpet Deep Clean module. When the robot detects carpet, it automatically lifts the mop pad and increases negative pressure suction to enhance deep carpet cleaning performance, improving dust removal by 40–50% compared to standard models.

Home size and runtime adaptation: For the common scenario of large single-family homes in the U.S., we upgraded battery capacity and optimized path planning for large-area cleaning. Our “charge while washing” design allows the robot to charge while returning to the base station to wash the mop, extending effective runtime without increasing battery size and weight.

We also enhanced AI navigation powered by dual-camera vision to handle complex floor plans in open-concept homes and large villas.

Stain scenario adaptation: Our FlowWash hot water cleaning technology continuously cleans the mop with fresh hot water during cleaning, preventing secondary contamination from dirty mops. This is optimized for common U.S. household stain scenarios such as kitchen food spills, muddy paw prints, and water tracked in from pools.

Robot vacuums approach their ‘iPhone moment’

When you say “iPhone moment,” are you thinking of apps and a platform approach, increasing levels of autonomy, or something else?

The “iPhone moment” describes a maturity leap for the entire robot vacuum category, rather than an app ecosystem or platform business model.

Right now, robot vacuums are still in the “iPod stage”: they only address flat floor cleaning, and remain tech novelties for early adopters. Penetration in China stands below 10%, while roughly 15% in mature overseas markets — far below the 90%+ rate for mature home appliances like refrigerators and washing machines.

The category will hit the “iPhone moment” inflection point when product experience, reliability and cost all reach mature home appliance standards. At that point, robot vacuums will become a daily household necessity, and penetration will see explosive growth.

Alongside mass adoption, products will also evolve in parallel from flat floor-cleaning tools to full-space “housekeepers” with 3D cleaning and organizing capabilities — the embodied intelligence form we are working toward.

item.title: NVIDIA replaces CEO amid China AI and robotics concerns
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
NVIDIA is replacing co-founder Jensen Huang with Collette Kress as CEO and Harvey C. Jones as board chair as it faces trade scrutiny.

The post NVIDIA replaces CEO amid China AI and robotics concerns appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
NVIDIA says it will continue to support customers amid its leadership changes. Source: NVIDIA

After a tumultuous week that saw NVIDIA Corp.’s stock drop by about 18.5%, CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down. The company today said it has appointed Collette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO and investor Harvey C. Jones as its first board chair.

Huang, who is one of the most recognizable figures in AI, recently admitted to extramarital affairs including with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy, and Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare at NVIDIA.

“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Jensen Huang wrote in a statement on Nov. 8. “Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s board of directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.”

Huang co-founded NVIDIA in 1993, and it makes graphics processing units (GPUs) and software architectures that are the basis for much of advanced computing and AI today. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company has a market capitalization of about $4 trillion, and its simulation and other technologies are used in industrial manipulators, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and emerging humanoid robots.

Kress and Jones to provide business continuity

Kress has served as EVP and CFO of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. NVIDIA said that she has played a key role in its growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft.

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” stated Kress. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and venture investor for more than 30 years. He has served as CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Jones about Kress. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

Submit your innovation now!

NVIDIA to endure competitive scrutiny

China leads the world in robotics manufacturing and usage, but it still relies on U.S. AI chips and edge computing components. Amid heightened trade conflicts, NVIDIA has worked with numerous global humanoid developers, including Unitree Robotics and Alibaba Cloud. Recent revelations about possible circumvention of U.S. export controls could lead to further investigations and reputational damage.

But in the meantime, NVIDIA has continued to support the robotics industry. Just this week, NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2, an updated open frontier world action model, and Isaac Lab 3.0, the latest version of its open-source robot learning framework. Huang spoke at GTC Berlin last month (see video below).

In September, NVIDIA said it planned to acquire Hugging Face Inc.’s open AI development platform for $12.9 billion. Pollen Robotics, a Bordeaux, France-based subsidiary of Hugging Face, had developed the Microduck open-source legged robot, which uses a Chinese processor.

NVIDIA last month described how robots such as Microduck could use its Isaac Lab learning framework, Newton physical modeling, Omniverse libraries, and Isaac Sim simulation for evaluation. Its deal with Hugging Face will receive more scrutiny, and competitors such as AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, and Intel may try to position themselves are more reliable Western suppliers.

Reuters and Monrningstar noted that Huang’s departure could slow deals around AI. The departure of a prominent tech exec could also lead to greater government scrutiny of trade deals as efforts continue to build so-called sovereign AI and robotics. The Robot Report will continue tracking these developments.

item.title: Viam Launchpad aims to accelerate robotics deployments
item.dc:creator: Oliver Mitchell
item.description:
The Viam Launchpad is intended to provide the software and engineering infrastructure to help startups bring robots to commercial deployment.

The post Viam Launchpad aims to accelerate robotics deployments appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Viam provides a software platform to ease robotics development. Source: Viam

Returning from RoboBusiness and RobOpsCon, I have never felt more optimistic about the robotics — I mean the physical AI — industry. Billion-dollar valuations and groundbreaking technology continue to outpace yesterday’s innovations at warp speed.

At the same time, too many brilliant entrepreneurs are languishing in taking their ideas from the lab to market. These startups, led by domain experts, are on a mission to automate their industries. However, they get stuck in ROS purgatory, unable to turn pilots into revenue-generating bots.

In 2020, Eliot Horowitz set out to create a better way to build and deploy smart machines. Drawing on his experience as co-founder and chief technology officer of MongoDB, Horowitz created Viam, a universal software abstraction layer for building and deploying hardware systems across enterprise fleets, or, as the company describes it, “The harness for physical AI.”

“In the past, robotics startups needed years of R&D and were faced with building a huge amount of infrastructure to make a project something more than a science experiment,” said Horowitz. “What we see with Viam is that a small team starting from zero can prototype in weeks or months, iterate, deploy, and capture real business with incredible velocity by leveraging Viam’s tools and harness for physical AI. We’re incredibly excited to be providing the ingredients needed to grow this new wave of robotics.”

From left: Florian Pestoni of InOrbit, Oliver Mitchell of Arkenstone Capital, Tiq Chapa of Google Cloud, and Betsy Mulé of F-Prime, at RobOpsCon’s VC panel. Source: Oliver Mitchell

Gambit gets a boost toward robotic kitchens

Since launching Viam, the platform has enabled numerous startups to launch and reach customers quickly, including Gambit, Tennibot, and Canyon Runner.

Horowitz and entrepreneur Nicole Maffeo co-founded Gambit. Now, Maffeo is taking her computer vision-based cooking guidance platform into a fully automated kitchen, complete with two robot arms located in the range vent to mix and stir an array of gourmet recipes.

Maffeo recently shared her experience working with Horowitz’s platform: “Partnering with the Viam engineering team over the last couple of years has truly catapulted Gambit forward. By pairing robust, enterprise-grade infrastructure with adaptable custom modules, the architecture empowers our team to transition seamlessly from initial hardware prototypes to real-world deployments. From telemetry and remote debugging to fleet management in field operations, Viam delivers the essential building blocks that allow us to move at incredible velocity.”

Conceptual design of Gambit’s robotic kitchen built on Viam’s software. Source: Gambit

Viam Launchpad provides immersive startup support

Now, Horowitz aims to build on top of Maffeo’s experience by establishing the Viam Launchpad. This six-month intensive program empowers founders with the technical and business tools to take their concepts from napkin drawings to commercial implementation.

As the advising executive director of the Launchpad, I can attest that the culmination of this incubator is not demo day, but installation day. This is possible because we fully immerse teams in Viam with usage credits, engineering support, and office space in the heart of New York City.

Unlike software, robotics founders need access to hardware, and Viam has one of the most robust robotics labs in the Northeast, complete with a robot arm farm. As a professional investor and author of A Startup Field Guide in the Age of Robots and AI, I also coach founders through a structured curriculum focused on building early customer-discovery feedback loops, refining go-to-market strategies, and leveraging an extensive network of mentors and investors.

Submit your innovation now!

RoboBuilt quickly preps for commercial deployment

Graduating from the Viam Launchpad, founders are propelled forward with a network of capital introductions, sales leads, and ultimately, purchase orders.

“Our ability to go from planning in a digital environment to physical robot actions within minutes, not days, is really incredible,” said Launchpad member Alex Gray of indoor construction robotics firm RoboBuilt. “ Viam’s modules for rudimentary actions let us focus faster on our specific tasks and avoid getting bogged down in basic setup of robot arm drivers and peripheral APIs.”

RoboBuilt co-founder Shean Rahman illustrated how the software and program are game changers. “We were working in Isaac Sim previously. It’s an incredibly deep and accurate program,” he said. “However, much of the physics, visualizations, and other components aren’t as crucial to our workflow as they may be for other applications.”

“Viam has so many basic initialization steps already mapped out; it lets us get to our core problem faster,” Rahman added. “We look forward to leaving the incubator with a working commercial deployment in time for our seed funding round.”

RoboBuilt founders Alex Gray and Shean Rahman at the Viam Launchpad. Source: Viam

F-Prime shares the state of robotics at RoboBusiness

At RoboBusiness last month, Sanjay Aggarwal of F-Prime Capital continued his annual tradition of presenting “The State of Robotics” report to the attendees. In essence, with so many mega rounds, the industry is very strong.

According to F-Prime’s data, automation investments this year have exceeded the past four years combined, surpassing $60 billion in just nine months. While most of this capital is still undiluted, the industry hopes the IPOs of Unitree and Agility will unleash a new spirit of unicorn exits and provide badly needed liquidity, driving a flywheel of invention for decades to come.

Avery Rosen, Viam’s technical chief of staff, asked Aggarwal, “Where do you still see opportunities for startups to innovate?”

The VC quickly answered, “Enabling technologies,” and pointed to his chart showing that only $1.3 billion is being invested in software to speed up robotics deployment. Avery, an integral part of the Viam Launchpad, noted that is exactly what Horowitz aims to disrupt.

The overall market for enabling systems is projected to climb to over $23 billion by 2031, part of a larger $78 billion robotics software market. Today, the industry is crowded with open-source options and large multinational providers racing to fill the void of seamless deployments.

Yet despite significant investment from technology giants like Google with Intrinsic and Amazon with RoboMaker, widespread adoption remains elusive. AWS shuttered RoboMaker last year after seven years of limited traction.

The 2026 State of Robotics Report breaks down investment categories. Source: F-Prime

ROS still requires development time

The most widely adopted open-source robotics framework remains Open Robotics’ Robot Operating System (ROS), with an estimated 1.3 million monthly users. NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim robotics simulation platform is also gaining momentum, surpassing 1 million cumulative downloads this year.

However, downloads and developers don’t necessarily translate into customer-facing rollouts. Viam recently demonstrated how its platform builds on NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim and Cosmos technologies to connect synthetic data generation and AI model training with real-world applications. This more comprehensive approach, combining hardware-agnostic software infrastructure with hands-on engineering support, is helping bridge the gap between simulation, prototype, and deployment, a critical step toward making physical AI a commercial reality.

The Viam Launchpad Robotics Lab in New York. Source: Viam

Next year, ROS will celebrate its 20th anniversary, the work of Morgan Quigley and his colleagues at Stanford, followed by Willow Garage, which first developed the software. Today, the open-source platform remains a collection of independently developed modules.

While Open Robotics has provided enormous opportunities for roboticists, we have leaned on ROS as the foundation for production-grade robotics for too long, pushing it to handle tasks it was never designed to address on its own. ROS 2 is a major leap forward over its predecessor, but the capital, time, and resources required to convert prototypes into enterprise-level deployments still hold the industry back, especially for developers without mechanical engineering resources.

Just as the iPhone and App Store democratized mobile app development, Viam is helping usher in a similar moment for robotics by lowering the barriers to building and scaling hardware startups.

Over the past 15 years, accelerators have empowered disruptors to conquer markets coast to coast, from YC in California to ERA in New York. While amazing companies have thrived, robotics requires a different approach, not just office space and equipment, but also deep technical and commercial enablement.

This is the thesis behind the Viam Launchpad: empowering a new generation of robotics founders with deep industry expertise to solve real problems through automation. These problem solvers are in a hurry and don’t have time to tinker with drivers, integrations, and software modules. They demand an easier way, an abstraction layer that allows them to focus on serving paying customers.

To learn more and apply to the Viam Launchpad, click here.

item.title: Runway’s Praxis-1 world action model for robotics is now available
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Runway launched Praxis-1 with partners including Noble Machines, Standard Bots, and Ultra. Developers can now use it with open weights.

The post Runway’s Praxis-1 world action model for robotics is now available appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Praxis-1 builds on Runway’s work as a founding member of the Cosmos Coalition, advancing open world models for physical AI. | Source: Runway

Runway AI Inc. yesterday released Praxis-1, its world action model for robotics. The model is now available to developers with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license.

Runway first announced Praxis-1 in September with launch partners including Noble Machines, Standard Bots, and Ultra. Since then, these companies have been running the model on their own hardware, including a legged humanoid, a six-axis industrial arm, and a dual-arm warehouse robot.

“A strong base model goes a long way. Earlier, with Noble Machines, our previous model needed a lot of training to learn their warehouse task: picking up wooden planks one at a time and placing them in a container,” Andy Chen, the head of robotics at Runway, told The Robot Report. “Praxis-1, built with more compute and data, learned it from half an hour of examples and got it right 15 times out of 15. Then we gave it a messy pile of planks it had never seen to clear into bins, and it cleared the whole pile six times out of 10.”

“Iterating on feedback from partners makes our models better,” he continued. “Today, Praxis-1 is the top-ranked world action model on NVIDIA’s RoboLab leaderboard, and the top-ranked open-source, end-to-end policy.”

Praxis-1 is available on GitHub, on Hugging Face with native LeRobot support, and in vLLM-Omni, with hosted inference on Reactor. Runway said it released everything developers need to run and adapt the model on their own hardware under Apache 2.0, including for commercial use. That covers the weights and the inference and fine-tuning code, with support for both full fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation (LoRA).

Praxis-1 runs out of the box across NVIDIA hardware, from data center GPUs such as the H100 and B200, to workstation GPUs like the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000, to Jetson Thor on the robot itself.

Praxis-1 builds on Runway’s video foundation models

Praxis-1 is a 27B-parameter mixture-of-experts diffusion transformer that predicts video and actions together.

On RoboLab-120, Praxis-1 reached 46.2% success across 1,200 episodes, compared with 42.9% for FLUX 3 Action, 36.8% for Cosmos3 Nano and 28.0% for π0.5. It ranks fifth overall on the leaderboard.

“The core piece is that a model trained to predict video really understands a lot about the physical world: how objects behave, how hands move, what a task looks like partway through, and so on,” Chen said.

“Praxis-1 is built on Runway’s video foundation model, and it learns how the world works before it learns to act,” he added. “We keep video prediction in the training objective the whole way through, so the model pictures what the scene should look like next and produces the motion that gets it there.”

Praxis-1 works across different robot embodiments

Praxis-1 learns how objects behave and how tasks unfold from large-scale video. | Source: Runway

Praxis-1 learns how objects behave and how tasks unfold from large-scale video, which gives it a head start on a new embodiment before fine-tuning on any hardware or domain-specific data, explained Runway. The company’s research has shown that web video matches teleoperated robot video as pre-training data for policy performance, which shifts the bottleneck on a capable policy to how much general video a model can learn from.

“The tasks vary with the robot. Noble Machines builds a legged humanoid for heavy industrial handling, and with them Praxis-1 picks up wooden planks, places them in containers and clears mixed piles into bins,” Chen said. “Standard Bots makes six-axis arms for factory work like machine tending and palletizing. Ultra builds and deploys dual-arm stations that pack orders in warehouses. A humanoid, a single arm, and a pair of arms are very different machines, and the same model drives all three.”

“With our partners, a single Praxis-1 checkpoint has adapted to a variety of embodiments with light fine-tuning, and with LoRA, you can adapt it to your own embodiment, cameras and tasks without retraining the full model,” said Runway. “Fine-tuned on Google’s RT-1 robot, which never appeared in its training data, Praxis-1 reaches 80.0% success on SimplerEnv, well above the original RT-1 policy at 52.4%.”

Submit your innovation now!

Why keep Praxis-1 open weight?

Runway has been committed to shipping Praxis-1 as an open weight model since its initial announcement. Open weights give hardware developers the flexibility to run, inspect, and adapt a world action model on their own terms, according to the New York-based company.

“At Runway, we believe that U.S. leadership in physical AI is critical,” Chen asserted. “Regaining our global lead in manufacturing, accelerating productivity across our economy, and securing ourselves and our allies will rely on this.”

“Achieving this will require a significant increase in investment across both hardware and software, but it will also require a level of interoperability and openness from American models that does not currently exist for physical use cases,” he said. “We view open world models as a compounding advantage that gives hardware developers flexibility and control they don’t currently have.”

After making Praxis-1 available to developers, Runway said it is focusing on scaling deployments.

“We want Praxis-1 in the real world: in real warehouses, factories, and industrial sites, doing real work,” Chen said. “We believe the frontier of robotics will be discovered through real-world applications, not in a lab. So what comes next is deploying with our partners, learning from what the model runs into out there, and putting those lessons back into the model.”

item.title: Serve Robotics opens robot delivery network for others to build on
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Serve Robotics says its on-demand delivery API allows third parties to develop new delivery services on its fleet of more than 2,000 robots.

The post Serve Robotics opens robot delivery network for others to build on appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The AV Delivery Developer Portal enables anyone to call robots from Serve’s delivery fleet. Source: Serve Robotics

Serve Robotics Inc. today launched the AV Delivery Developer Portal, which it said gives developers, businesses, hobbyists, and AI assistants the opportunity to programmatically summon its sidewalk delivery robots. The company said its public application programming interface, or API, allows others to work with its autonomous robot fleet. It also released a sandbox environment where anyone can build and test applications before using them with live robots.

“You shouldn’t have to start a robotics company to build something useful with robots,” stated Ali Kashani, co-founder and CEO of Serve Robotics. “We’ve spent years figuring out how robots can navigate neighborhoods. The people who live and work there will have needs we haven’t thought of. Opening our fleet gives us an opportunity to serve those needs.”

Spun out of Uber in 2021, Serve Robotics designs and operates robots that autonomously navigate complex, human-centric environments. The Redwood City, Calif.-based company said it has deployed more than 2,000 robots across the U.S. and Australia, reaching about 3 million people and supporting delivery for more than 4,000 restaurants.

Earlier this year, Serve acquired hospital service robot provider Diligent Robotics. Serve asserted that it designs its robot hardware and software to work safely in public and private environments at scale.

Serve Robotics opens tech to new robots, developers

Serve Robotics said its mobile robots are intended to make daily errands easy and on-demand delivery affordable and accessible. Businesses can use the robots to transport goods between their offices, and local businesses can expand their delivery footprints without hiring more staffers, the company noted.

Last week, Serve launched Serve Physical AI Services, opening its technology to companies building new types of robots. While the company’s systems have completed hundreds of thousands of deliveries across more than 150 neighborhoods in 20 U.S. cities, they have been available only through third-party delivery partners — until now.

Today, Serve said it “opens the fleet itself to anyone needing affordable and efficient autonomous last-mile delivery.” Developers can build on their existing apps, businesses can add robots into their daily workflows, and AI assistants can carry out tasks in the physical world, it said.

The AV Delivery Developer Portal allows anyone to dispatch those robots with a few lines of code or even an AI agent. “The same robots previously only available through the largest delivery platforms can now power any local delivery,” said Serve Robotics.

Submit your innovation now!

Builders can use API and sandbox before live robots

“Building on the fleet works like building on any other API,” claimed Serve Robotics. An application or AI assistant can request a pickup and dropoff, confirm the details, and tracks a robot until the delivery is complete. Serve handles the dispatch, routing, navigation, and remote supervision to ensure a timely, safe, and reliable delivery.

Deliveries are limited to Serve’s active service areas and operating hours, as well as to items that fit within the robot’s cargo compartment.

The sandbox lets developers simulate robots, run delivery workflows, and rehearse edge cases before running real robots. Builders can explore the documentation and sandbox at https://developer.serverobotics.com.

Access to live robots is subject to Serve’s approval. Those who wish to move beyond the sandbox can indicate their interest via the portal, said the company.

item.title: Memories.ai builds standardized egocentric video pipeline
item.dc:creator: Mike Oitzman
item.description:
Memories.ai provides standardized egocentric video collection and AI-powered annotation to build training data infrastructure for robotics.

The post Memories.ai builds standardized egocentric video pipeline appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Memories.ai models label every clip: Memories-H0 for hand pose, EgoAction for action segments. | Credit: Memories.ai

Memories.ai is building a data pipeline for robotics companies that combines standardized video collection with AI-powered annotation to turn everyday egocentric footage into training data for robots.

The San Francisco-based company is developing software and AI to help robots understand the physical world. It builds video-understanding models and data infrastructure, and it collects and annotates first-person (egocentric) video to provide high-quality training data to robotics companies.

The longer-term aim is to be a data-infrastructure partner for robotics and physical AI, not just a data vendor.

Memories.ai builds platform on video data

Memories.ai claimed that its video data infrastructure platform is built for physical AI, robotics, world models, vision-language-action (VLA) models, and humanoids. It provides a curated video data lake featuring egocentric video, along with custom annotation services and dataset tools to train robot learning models.

The company obtains egocentric video through data collectors and partners, providing them with standardized capture hardware—described as a modular camera setup—and uniform process to collect footage in a consistent way.

Memories.ai then processes and annotates the data with its models and makes it available through its data infrastructure. The company has published multiple elements of its research on its GitHub repo. It has also published at the ICLR, NeurIPS, and EMNLP events.

Submit your innovation now!

NVIDIA Cosmos helps realize physical AI vision

“Our vision right now is to accelerate physical intelligence, and our vision is to stand really at the frontier to being able to be part of the robotics game,” Shawn Shen, co-founder and CEO of Memories.ai, recently told The Robot Report. “We really bring robotics into the actual physical world, and I believe that’s our whole team’s vision. And whatever can help us to make that vision come faster, we’re happy to do it.”

Shen said the company is focused on processing its own data, rather than collecting video from a wide range of devices and sources. Once it gets data from partners, Memories.ai processes and annotates the footage itself.

The company said last month that it has used NVIDIA Cosmos to interpret video entering its data lake. It then curates that data to post-train Cosmos for customers’ robotics and industrial applications. This loop turns real-world video into models tailored to the tasks our customers need to solve.

Pipeline has a modular design

Memories.ai said its setup is modular to support diverse tasks and camera views. Shen asserted that the company wants to grow with the industry as AI models mature for more robotics applications.

“We want to be long-term partners,” he said. “We don’t want to just sell you the data. In the future, we want to work with you on the models. We want to work with you on the infra because we know that you are, and will be, limited by your resources too.”

For robotics customers, Memory AI plans to tailor the data to their needs, offer exclusive or non-exclusive arrangements, and potentially expand its role into models and video infrastructure.

item.title: Can AI agents program industrial robots without training data? Berkeley says yes
item.dc:creator: Mike Oitzman
item.description:
UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools for teams of AI coding agents that write, simulate, and refine readable robot programs. 

The post Can AI agents program industrial robots without training data? Berkeley says yes appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The new RoboSimStudio is an open-source project that enables agentic AI coding of robotic simulation environments. | Credit: UC Berkeley

UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools for a new approach: enabling teams of AI coding agents to write, simulate, and refine readable robot programs.

Since the early days of industrial robots, programming, tuning, and troubleshooting robotic workcells has taken weeks to months. New research coming out of UC Berkeley has demonstrated that new agentic AI programming tools could change how industrial robots are coded and maintained.

Why is this important? As anyone who’s programmed an industrial workcell knows, implementing the code has to wait until the end of the design and fabrication process. The robot needs to be installed in the workcell; all of the feeders, conveyance, and other elements also need to be installed. The pressure to get this done all falls on the software team, often when the project deadline is looming.

The new toolset goes beyond the idea of “vibe coding” a robot application. While it generates code with large language models (LLMs), what’s novel is the use of AI agents to manage the coding, testing and deployment.

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are programmed,” said Ken Goldberg, the William S. Floyd Jr. Distinguished Chair in Engineering at UC Berkeley. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test, and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

Researchers introduce GaP and VABAR

  • Graph-as-Policy (GaP) is a modular framework that splits a task into skills — perception, grasp planning, collision-free motion — which agents generate, connect and rehearse in simulation.
  • Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR) is a benchmark of six tasks: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. It is built built on Isaac Lab-Arena and Newton, with standardized variations and difficulty tiers.
  • The UC Berkeley and NVIDIA team presented the concept at CoRL 2026 this week in Austin, Texas.

How the toolset works

Dr. Goldberg described the research to The Robot Report. In September, Eric Chen, one of his graduate students, give GPT-6 Astra Eric’s new RoboSimStudio tool to see if it could generate not just a graphic model, but also a full 3D simulation of a scene. And that’s exactly what happened.

According to Goldberg, Chen gave the model a video and this new tool, and within an hour, it had generated a Newton simulation that was incredibly similar to the video.

“When a new frontier model came out in early September, they gave it the tool and a video,” said Goldberg. “Within about an hour, it produced a Newton simulation closely matching the video, by iterative trial and error.”

“And Newton [simulation] is really wonderful,” he added. “The problem is Newton is very complicated. It has a lot of parameters, hundreds of parameters. So generally, people didn’t really use it that much because it’s just too complicated, too many dials and switches.”

Goldberg praised Chen for pulling this together. Initially, Chen built the tool just for himself.

“I want my student Eric to get credit for this,” he said. “He basically sat down and built a new interface for Newton called RoboSimStudio. It is basically just an interface that makes you have sliders on the right-hand side of your screen, and you have a visualizer on the left. … You can tune all these parameters much easier than you could before, so he built that just for himself to make the simulation part easier.”

But simulation alone isn’t enough, according to Goldberg. Simulation matters to the whole approach of using agents to code robots.

“The agent needs a simulator to be able to basically iterate and see how to improve this code,” he said. Goldberg noted that the existing tools “were not very reliable and had a lot of problems.”

The harness converts a VA task specification into a computation graph, optimizes it via self-learning in simulation, and hands G* to an edge-based interpreter that drives the robot — sim and real feedback close the loop. | Credit: UC Berkeley

Agents write and test code

Agentic robotics operates in a loop: Agents write robot code, test it in simulation, see where it fails, and revise. That loop is only as good as the simulator behind it.

Newton Physics, the open-source physics engine that UC Berkeley chose, is powerful but exposes hundreds of parameters, which has kept many developers from using it.

RoboSim Studio made those parameters tractable, and that turned the simulator from a bottleneck into something an AI agent could tune on its own.

UC Berkeley developed the VABAR benchmark suite with NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena open-source policy-evaluation framework and the Newton physics engine. It includes a detailed physics-based simulation for contact-rich robot-object interactions.

VABAR evaluates how robots perform on practical manipulation tasks ranging from tool sorting and handing to cable insertion and routing. The tool facilitates comparisons and measures progress across realistic industrial tasks, changing conditions, and increasing levels of difficulty.

Each task includes standardized variations, difficulty tiers, and success metrics, allowing researchers to measure progress, compare approaches, and evaluate whether systems can handle the demands of industrial operation. At the same time, Isaac Lab-Arena enables large-scale systematic evaluations across changing task conditions.

Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at NVIDIA (and son of CEO Jensen Huang), has worked with Goldberg’s lab at UC Berkeley to interface with the NVIDIA product teams.

The partners listed some of the new capabilities:

  • Graph structure: Each node (perception, grasp, motion planning) can be assigned to its own agent, so agents work in parallel without “stepping on each other’s toes.”
  • ROS equivalence: The graph turns out to be equivalent to a ROS graph and can be converted to ROS 2.
  • Output: Python that calls existing vendor modules (such as KUKA) for low-level drive control. It does not replace robot controllers.
  • The harness: Thousands of prompts and structures constrain the agents.

How do agents change robot programming?

When asked how this new approach differs from straight “vibe coding” of an app, Goldberg responded that the magic is in the harness provided by GaP. The graph structure organizes the agents.

The code produced by “vibe coding” is already mature and well understood, he explained. The use of AI to write code is accepted in software engineering today. But rarely does an application function as intended in the first pass.

This is true for software from human engineers, and it’s equally true for software development developed with AI. Testing and iteration are needed to optimize the application, said Goldberg.

When applied to robotics, the best practice now is to test in simulation before deploying the code on a real robot. With agentic AI, a robotics engineer can enable the agent to iterate on both the simulation environment and then the subsequent code to more efficiently develop the robotic application.

For instance, Bosch is evaluating agentic robotics for diverse industrial automation scenarios. “Agentic robotics holds great promise because it generates interpretable code that engineers can thoroughly analyze before production deployment,” said Liu Ren, senior vice president and AI fellow at Bosch Research. “Bosch Research is actively collaborating with Goldberg and Huang and their teams.”

“AI-powered industrial robots must continuously improve reliability and performance,” said Jeff Mahler, co-founder and chief technology officer of Ambi Robotics. “Agentic robotics converted production data into robot behavior updates, increasing throughput across our U.S. fleet while keeping engineers in control.”

Goldberg is also an advisor to Ambi Robotics.

item.title: Dynamic Creatures partners with Sixth Wall Studio to bring Hasbro characters to life with robots
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
The companies will combine Sixth Wall’s character authoring and alignment with Dynamic Creatures’ mobile, expressive robots.

The post Dynamic Creatures partners with Sixth Wall Studio to bring Hasbro characters to life with robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
On the left, Roberta Thomson, the CEO of Sixth Wall Studio, and on the right, Marc Theerman, co-founder and CEO of Dynamic Creatures. | Source: Dynamic Creatures

Dynamic Creatures today said it has partnered with Sixth Wall Studio, an AI studio launched by Hasbro in June 2026. The collaborators plan to bring Hasbro characters to life through interactive robots.

The company will combine its mobile, expressive robots with Sixth Wall‘s character authoring and alignment. The goal is to create characters that can greet guests, share adventures with them, and remember them when they return at theme parks, resorts, and other entertainment and hospitality venues.

“Today CharacterOS is focused on voice, and Dynamic Creatures is focused on the physical embodiment,” Marc Theermann, the co-founder and CEO of Dynamic Creatures, told The Robot Report. “Together, the partners will work on turning bits and bytes into real personality over time. One of the research areas is to turn answers into meaningful expressions.”

Through the partnership, Sixth Wall Studio will extend its CharacterOS platform and Behavioral Licensing framework into physical experiences. It will support how characters speak, behave and remain true to their established personalities and stories.

Dynamic Creatures said its robots will give that intelligence a physical presence. The company connects a character’s conversation and personality with expressive movements, gazes, gestures, reactions, and more.

“Bringing a character to life means preserving the personality, voice, and story that fans love while opening up new ways to interact,” said Roberta Thomson, CEO of Sixth Wall Studio. “Our partnership with Dynamic Creatures takes that ambition into the physical world. We envision characters that can share an adventure with you while feeling unmistakably authentic from the first hello.”

Dynamic Creatures designed its first character robot, Hugo, to move freely through guest environments. | Source: Dynamic Creatures

Partners plan to use robots to provide better guest experiences

Together, the companies envision encounters that become part of a continuing story. A character at a resort could welcome a guest, send them on a quest and, during a later encounter, ask how the adventure went. 

“One use case we are exploring is for a guest to show the robot their entrance ticket,” Theerman said. “This would allow the robot to identify the guest, and provide personalized experiences such as dining recommendations, or skip the line suggestions.”

Beyond theme parks and resorts, the partners envision applications across hotels, cruise ships, retail destinations, and other immersive environments. Memory-enabled experiences would be developed around guest choice and clearly defined permissions, with deployment details established for each venue and use case. Initial Sixth Wall applications would align with its focus on audiences ages 13 and older.

“Safety is a central pillar for both Dynamic Creatures and Hasbro,” said Theerman. “For Hasbro, it’s about safe interactions, and for Dynamic Creatures, it’s about physical safety of the robot. One way to ensure this today is by having a human in the loop. Over time, more autonomy features will be swapped in, and the human supervisor will go from teleoperation to telemonitoring.”

Dynamic Creatures has a busy few months since emerging from stealth

Dynamic Creatures emerged from stealth in September 2026 and is developing fully custom robots and character experiences built on existing robotic platforms. As Boston Dynamics’ official hospitality and entertainment partner, the Cambridge, Mass.-based company combines advanced mobility with character design and real-time interaction for guest environments.

Its SnowJay robotics AI platform coordinates perception, movement, and behavior, bringing together conversation, memory, facial expressions, and animatronics. The company recently released Hugo, its first living character robot. The robot runs on SnowJay and features 43 actuators.

“For generations, people have formed powerful connections with fictional characters. Now those characters can share our physical world and respond to us as individuals,” said Marc Theermann, co-founder and CEO of Dynamic Creatures. “Sixth Wall brings the character intelligence and creative framework. We bring the physical expression and presence. Together, we want to make meeting a favorite character feel like the beginning of an ongoing relationship.”

item.title: Why predictive maintenance matters more as factories add robots
item.dc:creator: Rob Carbone
item.description:
As robotics scales across industries, companies need a maintenance strategy to collect and use the right data to minimize downtime.

The post Why predictive maintenance matters more as factories add robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Robot data combined with predictive analytics can improve uptime and productivity, says ATS. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Factories are adding more robots because they can handle repetitive, precise, and physically demanding work at high speed. As robotics take on a greater share of production, keeping those systems available becomes more important.

The International Federation of Robotics (IFR) reported about 5 million industrial robots in operation worldwide in 2025, up 11% from the prior year.

An unexpected robot failure can affect more than one machine. It can interrupt a cell, slow a line, and create delays that spread through the plant. As manufacturers rely more heavily on robotic systems, the need to identify developing problems before they force equipment offline becomes increasingly valuable. 

Why robotic systems raise the support stakes

Traditional preventive maintenance follows a schedule based on time, usage, or manufacturer recommendations. That approach still has value, but it may not reveal what’s happening inside a robot between planned service intervals. A joint, reducer, motor, or controller can begin to show signs of wear while the robot is still operating. 

 Predictive maintenance uses equipment data to identify changes that may point to developing faults. NIST describes condition monitoring as the detection, diagnosis or prediction of faults and failures in industrial equipment. 

For robotics, that means maintenance decisions can be based more on actual equipment condition than on a calendar alone.

Submit your innovation now!

What predictive maintenance can monitor 

Industrial automation and related systems generate many types of operating data. Useful signals depend on the robot, application, and failure mode. Common examples include vibration, temperature, and motor current. Torque, controller alarms, cycle data, and maintenance history can also provide useful context. 

The goal isn’t to collect every available data point. Teams need data that can reveal changes tied to the way a robot operates. A rise in vibration may point to a mechanical issue, while changes in motor current or torque may indicate added resistance or abnormal loading. Temperature variations can also signal that a component isn’t operating as expected. 

Changes in an end effector, sensor, conveyor, or surrounding process can affect robot performance. Looking at the robot in the context of a larger workcell can help teams separate normal operating variation from a change that may deserve maintenance attention. That distinction is especially important if the same robot handles different loads, speeds, or motion paths. 

This is where reliability monitoring can help. Sensors and connected systems can gather machine data, while monitoring and analytics tools help identify changes in equipment behavior. When a pattern changes, maintenance teams can then investigate the cause before a failure forces the robot offline.

Changes in equipment performance, plus environmental or process data, can provide warning of problems, says ATI. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Turn robot data into maintenance decisions

Collecting data is only the first step. The information has to support a practical maintenance decision. A useful alert should help a team determine what needs attention, how urgent the issue is, and when the robot can be inspected without causing an unnecessary production interruption. 

This becomes more important as factories operate larger fleets of robots. Maintenance teams may not have time to inspect every asset at the same frequency. Predictive maintenance can help direct attention toward equipment showing signs of change while allowing healthy assets to remain in service. 

Earlier warnings can also improve parts planning. If a component shows signs of deterioration, teams may have more time to confirm the problem, locate the correct replacement part, and schedule work during a planned maintenance window.

Earlier warnings can reduce downtime and improve productivity, says ATS. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Getting ahead on productivity, asset life, and safety

The value of predictive maintenance goes beyond preventing unplanned stops. Finding issues early on can limit secondary damage and help manufacturers get more useful life from robotic assets. Planned repairs can also reduce the disruption that occurs when technicians must troubleshoot a failed robot during production. 

A planned maintenance window gives teams more control over when equipment is taken offline and serviced. That can support safer maintenance practices because technicians can prepare for the work instead of responding to an unexpected failure under production pressure. 

As more factories rely heavily on robotics, maintenance strategies need to account for how those systems perform throughout their service life. Predictive maintenance gives manufacturers a way to use equipment data, condition signals and analytics to identify developing issues earlier. When that information leads to timely inspection and repair, manufacturers can reduce unplanned downtime, protect robotic assets and keep production schedules more stable. 

About the author

Rob Carbone is vice president of operations at Advanced Technology Services. He is responsible for leading initiatives that help manufacturers improve equipment reliability, maintenance excellence, and customer success.

item.title: Intel and Altera expand collaboration to simplify sensor integration for physical AI
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Altera and Intel are working to make it easier to connect diverse sensors, turn data into real-time insights, and develop robotics.

The post Intel and Altera expand collaboration to simplify sensor integration for physical AI appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Altera and Intel are collaborating to accelerate the development of intelligent systems across industries.

Intel Corp. and Altera Corp. today said they are jointly developing flexible, real-time, sensor-bridge reference systems for edge and physical AI applications including robotics. By combining Intel compute, connectivity, and software with Altera field-programmable gate arrays or FPGAs, the companies said they aim to help manufacturers address the growing complexity of connecting, processing, and acting on real-world data across increasingly sensor-rich environments.

“Physical AI systems have to sense, decide, and act in real time, and the physical world demands accuracy, reliability, and safety,” stated Farhad Shafai, head of business solutions and marketing at Altera. “Altera FPGAs provide the sensor connectivity, data processing, and deterministic control that machines need to respond to the physical world, and they stay programmable as sensors and AI models evolve. Combining that with Intel’s compute and software is intended to give OEMs a flexible foundation to tailor systems to their needs.’

Founded in 1983, Altera provides high-performance, programmable compute and connectivity systems for a wide range of advanced and AI-enabled technologies. The San Jose, Calif.-based company claimed that it
is “the largest pure-play FPGA provider with a full-spectrum portfolio serving applications ranging from data centers and communications networks to critical embedded systems.”

Intel acquired Altera for $16.7 billion in 2015 and sold 51% of the company to Silver Lake last year.

Sensor-rich edge environments pose challenges for AI

“Edge and physical AI systems can require data from different sensors and interfaces to be brought together while meeting requirements for timing, performance, power and cost,” said Intel and Altera. “Some applications also require very high bandwidth or flexible form factors in which input/output (I/O) is located away from the compute board. Sensor data must then be streamed rapidly into memory for the host Intel processor to use across edge, robotics and other workloads.”

The companies said they plan to develop modular reference systems that combine Altera programmable hardware with a consistent Intel compute and software foundation. Their goal is to give equipment OEMs greater flexibility as applications, sensors, and workloads evolve, while helping them move more efficiently from prototype to deployment.

“As sensors multiply at the edge and through physical AI systems, our customers need a simpler way to turn real-world data into timely action,” said Dan Rodriguez, corporate vice president and general manager of the Edge Computing Group at Intel. “Together with Altera, we aim to give OEMs a flexible foundation that simplifies integration and helps them move faster from prototype to market deployment while meeting their needs across performance, power and cost.”

Submit your innovation now!

Altera, Intel to apply programmable, real-time processing

Intel and Altera said they plan to address multiple markets where real-time processing and programmable computing matter most. The companies intend to make resulting reference solutions accessible to developers through Intel’s Open Edge Platform software development kit (SDK) and an Altera SDK.

  • Robotics: The partners said they will combine Intel compute, connectivity, and robotics software with Altera FPGAs to address the increasingly complex sensing, timing, and real-time processing requirements of intelligent machines.
  • Healthcare: The companies are jointly developing a reference system targeting the stringent latency and real-time requirements of advanced healthcare equipment.
  • Aerospace and defense: Intel and Altera are collaborating to support next-generation mission systems, with a focus on size, weight, and power requirements for converged AI and signal-processing workloads.

Together, Intel and Altera said they will help OEMs move faster from prototype by reducing integration complexity and addressing performance, power, and cost requirements across a range of edge applications.
